person.name: Alan_Turing
person.summary: Alan Turing gave computation a mathematical form through the Turing machine and helped break German naval Enigma messages during World War II. He later designed early computer systems, proposed the imitation game, and developed a mathematical account of biological pattern formation.

conclusion: The Turing machine remains a basic model for studying algorithms and the limits of computation. Turing’s work continues to influence computer science, artificial intelligence, cryptography, and mathematical biology.

events.title: Born in Maida Vale, London
events.description: Alan Turing is born in Maida Vale, London, while his father is on leave from the Indian Civil Service in British India.

events.title: Begins Studies at Sherborne School
events.description: Turing enters Sherborne School as a boarder. He pursues mathematics and science in a school culture centered on classical studies.

events.title: Lost Christopher Morcom
events.description: Christopher Morcom dies from complications of bovine tuberculosis. Turing gives greater attention to mathematics and science after his friend’s death.

events.background:
Sherborne School’s teachers placed their highest value on classical education. Turing’s aptitude for mathematics and science won little respect from some of them. His headmaster warned his parents that a boy who became only a scientific specialist was wasting his time at a public school. Turing nevertheless worked through advanced problems in 1927 without having studied elementary calculus. At 16, he read Albert Einstein’s work and appears to have derived Einstein’s challenge to Newton’s laws from a text that did not state it outright. The friendship gave those private scientific interests a companion within the boarding school.

Morcom had introduced Turing to astronomy. In the letter sent to Morcom’s mother, Frances Isobel Morcom, Turing called him brilliant, charming, and unassuming. He wrote that he had regarded his own work and astronomy as interests to share with him. He also believed Morcom had felt something similar. The illness had been contracted years earlier through infected cow’s milk. Turing kept in touch with Mrs. Morcom for years after her son’s death. She sent him gifts, and he wrote to her, often on Morcom’s birthday.

On February 12, 1933, Turing wrote to Mrs. Morcom before the third anniversary. He told her that he would be thinking of Christopher and of her the following day. He said he was sure Christopher was as happy as he had been while alive. In another letter, Turing considered whether spirit could survive bodily death. He wrote that a living and awake body held a spirit firmly. He thought death ended the bodily mechanism that held it. He supposed that the spirit might find a new body immediately or later. His later views became atheistic and materialist, though the article says his beliefs at this point still included a spirit independent of the body.

Turing told Mrs. Morcom that he would put as much energy into his work as though Christopher were alive. He said that this was what Christopher would have wanted him to do. The connection with Mrs. Morcom remained part of his life long after Sherborne.

events.title: Graduated from King's College
events.description: Turing completed his mathematics degree at King’s College, Cambridge, with first-class honors. His senior dissertation proved a version of the central limit theorem.

events.title: Elected a Fellow of King's College
events.description: King's College elects Turing a Fellow after considering his dissertation on the Gaussian error function. He begins the Part III mathematics course at Cambridge that spring.

events.title: Publishes On Computable Numbers
events.description: Turing publishes On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the [[Entscheidungsproblem|Entscheidungsproblem]]. The paper proves that no general method can solve every instance of Hilbert’s decision problem.

event_class.title: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
event_class.publisher: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society
event_class.impact: The paper became a foundation for theoretical computer science by giving a formal model of computation and establishing limits on what algorithms can decide.

Entscheidungsproblem.explanation: Hilbert’s question of whether a general procedure can determine the truth of every statement in a formal logical system.

events.background:
At King’s College, Cambridge, Turing was working through questions raised by Kurt Gödel’s incompleteness theorems while completing Part III mathematics. David Hilbert had posed the decision problem in 1928. Max Newman received the first draft of Turing’s investigation in mid-April 1936. Alonzo Church had published a result reaching a similar conclusion that month through lambda calculus, a symbolic system for representing functions. Turing’s account used a deliberately spare model of a worker following written instructions. The paper ran to 36 pages when he completed it on May 28. It appeared in two installments, dated November 30 and December 23.

The central objects were machines that read and alter symbols on a tape under a finite table of instructions. Turing gave each machine a standard description made from a restricted alphabet. He also encoded such descriptions as numbers. A universal machine could read one of those descriptions and carry out the specified operations. This made a machine’s instructions into data that another machine could inspect and execute.

For the decisive argument, Turing considered a proposed machine that could classify every machine as either “circle-free,” meaning it would continue printing binary digits, or circular, meaning it would fail to do so. He then constructed a further machine that would use the classifier’s answers to assemble a diagonal sequence from the outputs of the machines judged circle-free. Applied to its own encoded description, the construction produced a contradiction. The assumed classifier could not exist. Turing then connected this result to formulas in Principia Mathematica. He showed that a general way to determine whether the associated formula was provable would yield the impossible machine classifier. The final conclusion on Hilbert’s question took only 64 words and symbols in the paper’s proof.

John von Neumann later credited the paper’s central idea as the source of the modern computer’s basic concept. The equivalence later established between Turing’s machines and Church’s lambda calculus became known as the Church–Turing thesis. Turing carried the work to Princeton, where he studied under Church from September 1936 to July 1938.

events.title: Completes Doctorate at Princeton University
events.description: At Princeton University, Turing completed his doctoral work under Alonzo Church. The dissertation examined formal mathematical systems in light of Gödel’s incompleteness theorem.

event_class.title: Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals

events.background:
Princeton’s mathematics and philosophy departments were a meeting place for work on the limits of formal proof and mechanical calculation. Church had developed lambda calculus, a symbolic way to represent calculation, and used it in 1936 to establish that Hilbert’s decision problem could not have a general solution. Turing spent most of September 1936 through July 1938 at Princeton as a Jane Eliza Procter Visiting Fellow. Alongside his logic research, he studied cryptology and constructed three stages of an electromechanical binary multiplier. John von Neumann sought to retain him as a postdoctoral assistant, but Turing returned to Britain.

Gödel’s result supplied the problem’s starting point. Any formal system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove. A mathematician may add that statement as a new axiom, creating a stronger system. The stronger system then has its own true but unprovable statement. Turing examined an endless progression of such systems through the ordinal numbers, including transfinite stages beyond every finite number. He used Cantor’s method of infinities in this investigation.

The dissertation also introduced relative computing through machines supplied with “oracles.” An oracle was a hypothetical source that could answer questions beyond the reach of an ordinary computing machine. This allowed problems to be compared by the extra information needed to solve them. Martin Davis later identified this use of oracles as highly influential in theoretical computer science, including work on the polynomial-time hierarchy. Church and Turing also established that lambda calculus and Turing machines had equivalent computing power, a result associated with the Church–Turing thesis.

events.title: Joined Bletchley Park
events.description: Turing joins the Government Code and Cypher School at [[Bletchley Park|Bletchley Park]]. He works with Dilly Knox on German Enigma communications.

Bletchley Park.explanation: A wartime British codebreaking center operated by the Government Code and Cypher School.

events.title: Designs the Bombe for Enigma
events.description: Turing designs the bombe to help find Enigma settings. Its approach builds on the prewar Polish bomba method.

images.caption: A Turing Bombe at Bletchley Park
images.creator: Ian Petticrew

event_class.title: Bombe
event_class.description: An electromechanical machine tested possible Enigma rotor settings against a suspected message fragment to eliminate impossible configurations.
event_class.impact: Bombes accelerated the search for Enigma settings used by German military networks.

Bombe.explanation: An electromechanical codebreaking machine that tested possible Enigma settings against a suspected piece of message text.

events.title: Takes Charge of Hut 8
events.description: Turing leads Hut 8 at Bletchley Park. The section works on German naval Enigma messages.

events.title: Develops Banburismus for Naval Enigma
events.description: Turing develops [[Banburismus]], a statistical method for reducing bombe work on German naval Enigma messages. Hut 8 uses the method to read naval traffic more quickly.

images.caption: Four-rotor German naval Enigma at Bletchley Park
images.creator: Magnus Manske

Banburismus.explanation: A statistical cryptanalytic method used at Hut 8 to reduce the number of Enigma settings that bombes had to test.

events.background:
German naval traffic posed a problem with immediate consequences at sea. The Navy’s Enigma procedures were more secure than those used by the German Army and Air Force. Hut 8 often needed three to seven days to read a naval message, which made the intelligence operationally useless. From March through June 1941, U-boat wolf packs sank 282,000 tons of shipping a month. The section had limited staff and too few bombes to keep pace with German changes. In October, Turing, Gordon Welchman, Hugh Alexander, and Stuart Milner-Barry wrote directly to Winston Churchill for more people and machines. Churchill ordered that their needs receive extreme priority. More than two hundred bombes were operating by the war’s end.

The method rested on a running measure of how strongly intercepted material supported a possible rotor sequence. Turing called the unit a ban, and one tenth of a ban a deciban. Accumulated evidence could eliminate rotor sequences before a bombe was assigned to test them. In 1941, I. J. Good found that German telegraphists showed preferences when adding dummy letters to message indicators selected from the Kenngruppenbuch. He checked broken messages for these preferences and found that a bigram table producing a commonly chosen dummy letter was likely the right one. His observation became part of the Hut 8 procedure.

Captured trawlers also yielded cipher equipment and code materials during 1941. By November, Hut 8 had helped reduce monthly shipping losses to 62,000 tons. Joan Clarke became the only woman in the section to practice the method. Hugh Alexander later called her one of Hut 8’s best Banburists. A four-rotor naval Enigma introduced in 1942 again blocked Hut 8’s reading of traffic until further work on captured code papers opened a way forward.

events.title: Joins the National Physical Laboratory
events.description: Turing joins the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington. He prepares plans for the Automatic Computing Engine, a stored-program electronic computer.

events.title: Completes the Automatic Computing Engine Design
events.description: At the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, Turing completes the Automatic Computing Engine design. The design sets out a stored-program electronic computer.

images.caption: Pilot ACE at the Science Museum, London
images.creator: Antoine Taveneaux

event_class.title: Automatic Computing Engine
event_class.description: A stored-program electronic computer design used high-speed electronic memory to hold instructions and numerical data for general-purpose calculations.
event_class.impact: The ACE design guided British postwar computer development and influenced later stored-program machines.

events.title: Joins Manchester's Computing Machine Laboratory
events.description: Turing joins Max Newman's Computing Machine Laboratory at the University of Manchester. He begins writing programs for early computers.

events.title: Proposes the Imitation Game in Mind
events.description: Turing asks whether machines can think. He proposes the imitation game, a written conversation in which a human judge tries to identify the machine.

event_class.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
event_class.impact: The imitation game became known as the Turing test. It remains a central reference point in discussions of machine intelligence.

events.background:
British researchers had discussed machine intelligence for roughly a decade before artificial intelligence became a named field in 1956. Turing had been considering computer intelligence by 1941 and used the phrase in 1947. Members of the Ratio Club, an informal circle of British cybernetics and electronics researchers, also treated the subject as a live question. The paper confined its attention to digital machines, which manipulate binary digits and rewrite them in memory according to simple rules. It treated such machines as universal in principle. Given sufficient memory and time, one digital computer could simulate any other digital machine.

The game had begun as a three-person party exercise. A male player and a female player communicated with an interrogator through written messages. The interrogator knew them only as X and Y and tried to determine their sex. The male player tried to produce the wrong identification, while the female player helped the interrogator reach the right one. Turing adapted this setup because typed messages removed clues from voice and appearance. He then framed a technical question about a particular digital computer, its storage capacity, speed, and program. The standard was a machine’s performance in the conversation, not a prior definition of thought.

The paper answered nine objections in detail. They included arguments from theology, human fear of machine intelligence, mathematical limits associated with Gödel’s work, consciousness, Lady Lovelace’s claim that machines could only follow orders, and the informality of human behavior. Turing also considered claims that machines lacked particular capacities, including kindness, humor, initiative, and learning from experience. He predicted that by about 2000, a computer with a storage capacity of about one billion units would perform well enough in a five-minute exchange that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 percent chance of making the right identification.

events.title: Convicted of Gross Indecency
events.description: Turing was prosecuted for homosexual acts in 1952. He accepted hormone treatment as an alternative to imprisonment.

images.caption: Facade of Manchester County Court Offices
images.creator: Anthony Parkes

events.title: Publishes a Theory of Morphogenesis
events.description: Turing proposes that a [[reaction-diffusion system]] can produce organized patterns from an even chemical state. Chemical reactions and diffusion create the changing concentrations in the model.

event_class.title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis
event_class.publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London
event_class.impact: The article helped establish reaction-diffusion models as a way to study biological pattern formation.

reaction-diffusion system.explanation: A mathematical model in which chemical substances react and spread through space at different rates, producing changing spatial patterns.

events.title: Dies at His Wilmslow Home
events.description: Turing dies from cyanide poisoning. An inquest rules his death a suicide.
